claims.text: An IP address names a machine's place on a network and one machine can have more than one; the older, still common form writes it as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots.
claims.source_hint: RFC 791 section 2.3 (addressing) and RFC 1122 section 3.2.1 — 32-bit IPv4 addresses, dotted-decimal notation

claims.text: A port number runs from 0 to 65535.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.1 — the 16-bit Source Port and Destination Port fields of the TCP header

claims.text: A loopback address is one every machine has for itself, which data never leaves; the name localhost stands for it, and in the four-number form it is usually 127.0.0.1 (all of 127.x.x.x is loopback).
claims.source_hint: RFC 1122 section 3.2.1.3 (g) — 127.0.0.0/8 is the internal host loopback address, must never appear outside a host

claims.text: The name `localhost` stands for the loopback address, and therefore means the machine running the command rather than any fixed machine.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6761 section 6.3 — the special-use domain name localhost resolves to the loopback address

claims.text: The private ranges are those starting `10.`, `192.168.`, and `172.16` through `172.31`; they are meant for use inside one network and machines on the public internet cannot reach them. The lab's `172.28.0.x` numbers are inside such a range.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1918 section 3 — private address space 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, not routed on the public internet

claims.text: At stage-0 the lab box is `172.28.0.12` and the database machine `172.28.0.11` on block `172.28.0.0/24`; `docker-compose.yml` publishes 8080:8080 on the lab box, so your own machine passes what arrives on its 8080 to the lab box's 8080.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang docker-compose.yml at stage-0 (services lab/db ipv4_address, ipam, lab ports); Docker docs, publishing ports (-p host:container)

claims.text: A process claims a port by asking the operating system and listening on it; normally the operating system refuses a later program asking for the same number on the same address while the first holds it. Programs can ask to share a number, but most, like the SSH server, do not.
claims.source_hint: POSIX bind() EADDRINUSE; socket(7) SO_REUSEADDR/SO_REUSEPORT (sharing by opt-in); live run of two `nc -4 -l` on one port and `nc -l 2222` in donhang-lab

claims.text: One process can hold several ports: at stage-0 Caddy holds 8080 and 8443 on the lab box; it runs beside the box sharing its addresses and ports, so it is absent from the box's process list, yet another program on the box that does not ask to share 8080 is refused.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0 (the :8080 and donhang.local:8443 sites) and outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/who-listens.txt; docker-compose.yml web network_mode service:lab

claims.text: The port a process held can be claimed by another program once that process is gone; the number is held, not owned.
claims.source_hint: POSIX close()/bind() — the address bound to a socket is released when the socket is closed

claims.text: At stage-0 the lab box's SSH server listens on 2222, Caddy on 8080 and 8443, nothing on 9999; who-listens.sh and two-servers.sh re-run themselves inside the lab box when started outside it, so their output comes from there.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/who-listens.txt; docker-compose.yml service lab (LISTEN_PORT 2222); who-listens.sh/two-servers.sh line 5 (lab-run.sh) at stage-0

claims.text: `nc -z` reports only whether something is there on the given machine and port.
claims.source_hint: nc(1) man page — the -z flag, zero-I/O mode, used for scanning listeners; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/who-listens.txt (each target prints open or closed)

claims.text: `db:5432` is open while `db` is not the lab box: at stage-0 the database runs on another machine of the lab network, `172.28.0.11`. The listing printed by the script is narrowed by `grep` to 2222, 8080 and 8443, so it says nothing about 5432 either way.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/network/who-listens.sh line 19 (the grep filter) and docker-compose.yml services lab/db at stage-0

claims.text: `netstat -tln` prints one line per listening address and port (socket), so 2222 on `0.0.0.0` and `::` shows twice; `0.0.0.0` in front of a port means every IPv4 address the machine has, not one particular address.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1122 section 3.2.1.3 (a) — 0.0.0.0 as the unspecified/wildcard address; netstat(8) Local Address column; netstat(8) busybox -t -l -n; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/who-listens.txt

claims.text: The listening entries written with colons are IPv6, a second family of addresses beside the four-number form.
claims.source_hint: RFC 4291 sections 2.2 and 2.5.2 — IPv6 text representation and the unspecified address ::

claims.text: In `two-servers.sh` (`-l` makes nc listen, `-4` keeps it to IPv4) two `nc` runs hold 9001 and 9002 at the same time, and a third asking for 2222 is refused with `nc: Address in use` and exit code 1.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/two-servers.txt in the example repository, captured by scripts/capture-output.sh; nc(1) OpenBSD netcat options -l and -4

claims.text: The operating system reports only which error happened; the words printed for it come from the program that prints them, so on another machine the same refusal may read `address already in use`.
claims.source_hint: musl libc strerror table (/lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 in the lab box holds "Address in use"; nc does not); POSIX bind() EADDRINUSE names only the error code

claims.text: A request for a port on a machine where no process is listening is turned away at once rather than left unanswered, which is why `nc -z -w 3` reports `localhost:9999 is closed` without waiting out its three seconds.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.5.2 — if the connection does not exist (CLOSED), a reset is sent in response to any incoming segment; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/who-listens.txt

claims.text: Inside the lab box nothing listens on 5432, so `localhost:5432` finds nothing there, while `db:5432` reaches the database machine `172.28.0.11`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang docker-compose.yml at stage-0 — db is a separate service with its own address; the lab box shares its network namespace only with the web service (network_mode: service:lab)

claims.text: `db` is a name the lab gives the database machine, and inside the lab network it stands for that machine's address.
claims.source_hint: Compose file reference, networks key — a service is reachable by its service name on the networks it joins; examples/don-hang docker-compose.yml at stage-0

claims.text: `${target%:*}` keeps the part of the value before the last colon and `${target##*:}` the part after it.
claims.source_hint: POSIX shell parameter expansion: ${parameter%word} removes the smallest suffix pattern, ${parameter##word} the largest prefix pattern; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/who-listens.txt

claims.text: A command ending in `&` runs in the background, so the script carries on while it keeps running.
claims.source_hint: POSIX Shell Command Language 2.9.3 Lists — asynchronous lists

claims.text: `$!` holds the process id of the most recent background command.
claims.source_hint: POSIX Shell Command Language 2.5.2 Special Parameters — !
